title: Crimp a tube lug onto a 16 mm² cable with a bench-held battery crimper, then lay the cable back on its rest
instruction: Crimp the cable lug sitting in the crimping tool onto the cable's stripped end, then lay the cable, lug on, back on its rest and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Terminating stranded power cables with crimped compression lugs, which then bolt onto breakers, busbars, transformers and motor terminals, is regular work for electricians (about 821,000 US jobs in 2025 per BLS; O*NET tasks "Connect wires to circuit breakers, transformers, or other components" and "Install ground leads and connect power cables to equipment, such as motors") and for electrical and electronic equipment assemblers, control-panel builders among them (246,300 US jobs). A battery hydraulic crimper with interchangeable dies is a standard tool of theirs for lugs of this size. The stripped end has to go fully into the lug's barrel and stay straight while the die closes, or the joint fails a pull test or overheats.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A battery hydraulic lug crimper (CM-300G: 75 kN, 16-300 mm2 dies, 17 mm stroke, 18 V 3.0 Ah pack; yellow and black, steel head) lies on its side in a bench holder: an 18 mm plywood base (35 x 33 cm) clamped to the table with two C-clamps, plywood saddles under the tool and two hook-and-loop straps over its body and battery (the kit weighs 10 kg packed; the robot's only loads on the tool are the cable's push and the trigger squeeze, balanced in the hand). Its axis runs across the table, 7.5 cm up. Its head is on the left, swivelled on its round neck so its opening faces up, the 16 mm2 die pair (both halves marked 16) centred 30 cm forward and 6 cm left of the centre line. Its body and 18 V pack lie to the right; its grip points away from the arms, the trigger at the top of the grip, the trigger's face 14.3 cm right of the die's centre and 6.2 cm from the grip's back. Squeezing the trigger 2.0 mm in (of its 8.5 mm travel; 6 N at rest, 8.4 N there, 16.2 N at its stop) runs the pump: the ram closes the die (3 s in the simulation); once it has closed, the tool's pressure valve opens and the ram goes back (2 s). Let go sooner, the ram stops. The trigger is checked once on a kitchen scale: the motor runs at no more than 2.0 kg (20 N). Cost: about US$210 in all, of which the crimper kit is US$110-125 (listed with dies for 16 to 300 mm2, two packs and a charger); the rest is ten lugs, 2 m of cable, the holder, guard and rests, and the two scales. (2) In the fixed half of the die lies a tinned-copper tubular cable lug for 16 mm2 cable (Klauke 3R8: barrel 5.5 mm inside, 8.5 mm outside and 13 mm long; a flat palm 15 mm wide with an 8.5 mm (M8) hole; 29 mm long, 9 g), its barrel running forward, its mouth facing the arms 6.5 mm in front of the die's centre, its palm on a 3D-printed PLA lug holder behind the head with its end against the holder's stop. (3) A guard of 3 mm clear polycarbonate on the base encloses the head: walls 13.2 cm tall from 2.75 cm in front of the die's centre to 4.8 cm behind it, and from 3.8 cm right of the centre line (the tool's neck passes through this wall) to 13 cm left of it, and a lid. Its front wall, 1.8 cm in front of the barrel's mouth, has a 22 mm square feed hole on the barrel's axis. The trigger and grip are outside the guard. (4) A loose 16 mm2 single-core PVC-insulated cable (H07V-R, stiff), 16 cm long, 7 mm across and 27 g, its last 13 mm stripped to its stranded copper conductor, 5.1 mm across (the strip length matching the lug's barrel), lies along the forward direction on two black ABS-plastic V-rests, its axis 3 cm above the table, its bare tip 21 cm forward and 16 cm left of the centre line, pointing forward. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. The crimp: the first time the ram closes the die fully (the trigger held in past its switch point until the die has closed, 3 s in the simulation); let go sooner, the ram stops short and no crimp is made. A good crimp: then the bare end 10.5 to 13.5 mm into the 13 mm barrel (all but at most 2.5 mm of the copper in; the insulation, too wide to enter, stops at the barrel's mouth) and the cable within 8 degrees of the barrel's axis. If the die first closes with no copper in the barrel, it crushes the barrel shut and no crimp can follow. Released: the trigger let go, the ram back and the die open, and both grippers' fingertip centres (TCPs) at least 4 cm from the trigger. Taken out: after the crimp, the cable's tip at least 5 cm from where the barrel's mouth was (out through the feed hole), the lug on it. On its rest: the cable's tip within 3 cm (across) and 1.5 cm (up or down) of where it lay, the cable within 20 degrees of lying along the rests. 1.0: a good crimp, released, taken out, laid back on its rests, and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm of its start); 0.5: any crimp with the bare end in the barrel; 0.25: the bare end pushed at least 6.5 mm into the barrel at some point; else 0.0. In a real trial: the crimp shows as the full hexagonal impression of the closed 16 mm2 die on the barrel, all six flats complete, checked by eye after the trial; a squeeze let go early, or a pack too flat to reach the pressure valve's setting, leaves a partial impression and counts as no crimp (the crimp force is set by that valve, not by the pack's charge). The depth is read with a caliper as the bare gap between the insulation's end and the barrel's mouth (a 13 mm strip in a 13 mm barrel: a gap of at most 2.5 mm means at least 10.5 mm in); the cable's angle, the trigger, the ram, the rest position and the arms are read from the overhead video; and a good crimp must also pass a pull test: the lug holds a steady 450 N pull on the cable (the UL 486A pull-out force for this size). The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the trigger and the cable still.
reset_notes: Let go of the trigger so the ram goes back; lift the guard's lid, open the head's latch, lay a fresh Klauke 3R8 lug in the fixed half of the 16 mm2 die (both halves marked 16) with its palm on the lug holder against the stop, close the latch and the lid; lay a fresh cable, stripped 13 mm with its strands twisted tight, on its rests. Start each session with a charged pack (the kit has two) and check that the holder's straps and clamps are tight.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). The crimp is an event: when the die has closed, the task file reads where the cable's bare end is and, if it is in the barrel, swaps the lug for a crimped one that then goes where the cable goes (its hold isn't simulated). The cable is a stiff rod; the lug is fixed in the die. The hydraulics aren't modelled: the sprung trigger runs the shown ram over its 17 mm stroke in 3 s. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
